title: Albion
description: Placard data for the Albion wing: Victorian England from 1848 to 1898, the Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood and those who followed it, and the Arts and Crafts of William Morris and his circle. All works are in the public domain; images and sources are in assets/albion/paintings.

works.title: Mariana
works.notes: Tennyson's Mariana, left waiting in the moated grange, stretches after a day at her embroidery. The autumn leaves on the table and floor were painted one by one.

works.title: The Pretty Baa-Lambs
works.notes: Painted out of doors in full summer sun at Stockwell, with Emma Hill, soon to be Brown's wife, as the mother. Critics at the Royal Academy in 1852 were puzzled by a picture that seemed to tell no story.

works.title: Ophelia
works.notes: Ophelia floats singing down the stream before she drowns. Millais painted the bank of the Hogsmill in Surrey over five months, then Elizabeth Siddal in a bath of water in his London studio.

works.title: An English Autumn Afternoon
works.notes: The view from Brown's lodgings in Hampstead, looking south-east across back gardens towards Highgate. Asked by Ruskin why he had chosen such an ugly subject, Brown answered that it lay out of a back window.

works.title: The Awakening Conscience
works.notes: A kept woman rises from her lover's lap, struck by a memory as he sings. The mirror behind her shows the sunlit garden she has lost.

works.title: The Last of England
works.notes: An emigrant couple look back from the deck as the English coast falls away; Brown and his wife Emma sat for them. He painted much of it out of doors in winter to get the cold light and the raw hands.

works.title: The Blind Girl
works.notes: A blind travelling musician rests by the road near Winchelsea while the child beside her turns to look at a double rainbow. Millais first painted the colours of the outer bow in the wrong order, and corrected them later.

works.title: The Stonebreaker
works.notes: A labourer lies dead of exhaustion on a hillside at dusk, his hammer still in his hand. It was shown in 1858 with a passage from Carlyle on the toil-worn craftsman.

works.title: The Long Engagement
works.notes: A curate and his fiancée meet in a wood, still too poor to marry. The name Amy, carved long ago in the tree trunk, is being grown over by ivy.

works.title: Walton-on-the-Naze
works.notes: A summer evening on the Essex coast, with Brown's wife and daughter on the path and a rainbow over the fields. The family had spent a holiday there in 1859.

works.title: Morgan-le-Fay
works.notes: The enchantress, King Arthur's half-sister, prepares a magic robe meant to destroy him. She wears a leopard skin over her dress.

works.title: Medea
works.notes: The sorceress prepares a poison, her fingers at her coral necklace, against a ground of gold. The Royal Academy turned the picture down in 1868 and hung it the following year.

works.title: The Lady of Shalott
works.notes: Having looked out towards Camelot and brought the curse upon herself, the Lady drifts downriver, the candles in the boat almost out. The tapestry trailing in the water is the one she had been weaving.

works.artist: Morris & Co., after Edward Burne-Jones, with William Morris and John Henry Dearle
works.title: The Attainment: The Vision of the Holy Grail to Sir Galahad, Sir Bors and Sir Perceval
works.medium: Wool and silk tapestry on a cotton warp
works.notes: Galahad kneels before the Grail, guarded by angels; Bors and Perceval, who came with him, remain behind. The series was first woven for Stanmore Hall; this weaving was made at Merton Abbey for Laurence Hodson of Compton Hall.

works.title: King Cophetua and the Beggar Maid
works.notes: The king of the old ballad, who had vowed to marry no one until he found a beggar he could love, sits below her with his crown in his hands.

works.title: Beata Beatrix
works.notes: Rossetti's memorial to his wife, Elizabeth Siddal, painted as Dante's Beatrice at the moment of her death; a red dove drops a poppy into her hands. Siddal had died of a laudanum overdose in 1862.

works.title: Lady Lilith
works.notes: A reduced replica of Rossetti's oil of Lilith, Adam's first wife, combing her hair before a mirror. It keeps the face of Fanny Cornforth, which Rossetti later painted out of the oil in favour of Alexa Wilding's.

works.title: Proserpine
works.notes: Proserpine, held in the underworld, holds the pomegranate whose seeds bind her there. Jane Morris sat for her; this is the seventh of eight versions Rossetti began.

works.title: The Love Song
works.notes: A knight listens as a woman plays a small organ, its bellows worked by the winged figure of Love. The title comes from the refrain of an old Breton song.

works.title: Pygmalion and the Image: The Heart Desires
works.notes: The first of four panels. The sculptor Pygmalion broods in his studio, unmoved by the real women passing in the street outside.

works.title: Pygmalion and the Image: The Hand Refrains
works.notes: The second panel. The statue is finished, and Pygmalion stands back from the figure he has made and fallen in love with.

works.title: Pygmalion and the Image: The Godhead Fires
works.notes: The third panel. Venus comes down to the empty studio and brings the statue to life.

works.title: Pygmalion and the Image: The Soul Attains
works.notes: The last panel. Pygmalion kneels before the living woman, Galatea. Burne-Jones painted this second series between 1875 and 1878.

works.title: The Golden Stairs
works.notes: Eighteen young women with musical instruments come down a curving stair, to no stated purpose. Burne-Jones used the daughters of friends as models, among them his own daughter Margaret and May Morris.

works.title: Dreamers
works.notes: Three women doze on a long couch in the heat. Moore built the picture as an arrangement of colour and pattern rather than a story.

works.title: Love's Messenger
works.medium: Watercolour, tempera and gold paint on paper
works.notes: A woman at an open window takes a letter brought to her by a dove. Spartali Stillman, a pupil of Ford Madox Brown, worked mainly in watercolour.

works.title: Portia
works.notes: Portia from The Merchant of Venice, dressed in the red robes of a doctor of law. The actress Kate Dolan posed for her.

works.title: Flora
works.notes: The goddess of flowers stands before an orange tree, scattering roses. It was painted in Florence for the Liverpool collector William Imrie, and the scroll at her feet names the city.

works.title: Lachrymae
works.notes: A woman in black mourns against a Doric column topped by a funeral urn, with cypresses and a low sunset behind. It was among the last pictures Leighton showed before his death in January 1896.

works.artist: William Morris, with birds by Philip Webb
works.title: Trellis
works.medium: Block-printed in distemper colours on paper
works.notes: Morris's first wallpaper design, drawn in 1862 from the rose trellis in the garden of Red House; Philip Webb drew the birds. Printed by Jeffrey & Co. from pearwood blocks.

works.title: Acanthus
works.medium: Block-printed in distemper colours on paper
works.notes: Large curling leaves in close tones of one colour. It needed thirty separate blocks and was one of the dearest papers Morris & Co. sold.

works.title: Willow Bough
works.medium: Block-printed in distemper colours on paper
works.notes: Drawn from the willows along the river at Kelmscott. It has been printed almost continuously since.

works.title: The Star of Bethlehem
works.notes: The Magi bring their gifts to the Virgin and Child under a star held by an angel. Commissioned by the Corporation of Birmingham, it is among the largest watercolours of the century; the design had first been made for a Morris & Co. tapestry at Exeter College, Oxford.

works.title: Charger
works.notes: Two fish circle in the well of the dish, with more fish and leaves on the wide rim. De Morgan spent years recovering the lustre technique of Renaissance and Islamic potters.

works.title: Dish with an eagle
works.medium: Earthenware with lustre on a blue ground
works.notes: An eagle with raised wings against a thicket of copper-lustre leaves. Made at the Sands End pottery in Fulham, the works De Morgan ran from 1888 until 1907.

works.title: Vase with cover
works.notes: Winged beasts chase one another round the body in ruby lustre. The lustre is a thin film of copper, left on the glaze when the painted pigment is fired in a smoky kiln.

works.title: Dish with a peacock
works.notes: A peacock spreads its tail across the whole face of the dish in blues and greens. De Morgan called this palette Persian, after the Iznik pottery then thought to come from Persia.

works.artist: William Morris (Kelmscott Press), with woodcuts after Edward Burne-Jones
works.title: The Works of Geoffrey Chaucer Now Newly Imprinted
works.medium: Printed in black and red in Chaucer type on handmade paper, with wood-engraved illustrations
works.collection: Cleveland Museum of Art, Ingalls Library
works.notes: The largest book of Morris's Kelmscott Press, with eighty-seven illustrations after Burne-Jones set in borders by Morris. Burne-Jones called it a pocket cathedral; Morris saw it finished a few months before his death.

works.title: The Story of Tristram and Isolde
works.medium: Stained and painted glass, thirteen panels
works.notes: Thirteen panels made for Walter Dunlop's house, Harden Grange, near Bingley. The designs were shared out among the firm's partners and friends, including Morris, Rossetti, Burne-Jones, Ford Madox Brown and Arthur Hughes.

works.title: Rice dish
works.notes: Winged monsters chase one another round the wide rim, and a single one coils in the well, all in golden-brown lustre. The base is painted with De Morgan's mark and the initials of the decorator, Charles Passenger.

works.title: Plate with a ship
works.notes: A galley under sail, its oars dipped, passes a colonnaded harbour, with fish swimming in the waves below. De Morgan designed it and Charles Passenger, one of his decorators, painted it.

works.title: Dish with a great fish
works.notes: A great fish with feathered fins curls round the dish in a shoal of small ones. It was made at De Morgan's works in Chelsea, and borrows its motifs and its lustre from the pottery of the Near East.

works.title: Jar with two fish
works.notes: Two stylised fish face each other across the body of this two-handled jar, their bodies following the swell of the pot. It was made at Sands End, De Morgan's pottery in Fulham.
